pedagogy.summary: Direct proportion means two quantities keep a CONSTANT RATIO: as one is multiplied by k, so is the other, and their graph is a straight line THROUGH THE ORIGIN (y = kx). Inverse proportion means the PRODUCT is constant: as one is multiplied by k, the other is divided by k (xy = c, a curve). The pedagogical heart of the topic is (1) making the multiplicative structure of direct proportion explicit against merely additive change, and (2) resisting the 'illusion of proportionality' — the reflex to treat every relationship as directly proportional. Children must learn to ASK whether doubling one quantity really doubles the other, or halves it, or does neither.
bestPractices: Contrast three situations side by side — directly proportional (4 pens £6 → 10 pens £15, line through origin), inversely proportional (workers vs time to dig a hole; taps filling a bucket), and neither (phone plan £15/month + £0.20/min: linear but NOT proportional because the line misses the origin). Sorting situations into these three bins is the key discrimination.

Use the 'if one is zero the other is zero' test for direct proportion, and the 'doubling one halves the other' test for inverse — make the defining property a checkable question, not a memorised label.
Build direct proportion from ratio tables and double number lines so unit rate (cost per pen) is visible; scale up by multiplying, never by adding a constant difference.

Graph both: direct proportion is a straight line through the origin; inverse is a smooth decreasing curve. Reading the origin behaviour off a graph is a fast diagnostic of which (if either) relationship holds.
Delay the formulae y=kx and xy=c until the ratio-table and product-constancy reasoning is secure, so children reason about structure rather than substituting into a triangle.
keyRepresentations: Ratio table / double number line (direct proportion — scale columns by multiplying)
Graph through the origin (direct: straight line) vs decreasing curve (inverse)
Product-constant table for inverse proportion (e.g. speed×time = distance held fixed)
Three-bin sorting mat: directly proportional | inversely proportional | neither
commonMisconceptions: Illusion of proportionality — treating every relationship as directly proportional, applying y=kx to situations that are linear-but-not-proportional (phone plan with a fixed charge) or inverse.
Confusing direct and inverse: expecting 'twice as fast' to mean 'twice the time' rather than half the time.
Additive rather than multiplicative scaling: going from 4 pens to 8 pens by adding the same amount to the cost instead of doubling it.
Believing any straight-line graph shows direct proportion, ignoring whether it passes through the origin.

learn.summary: Direct proportion means two quantities keep a constant ratio: multiply one by k and the other is multiplied by k, so the graph is a straight line through the origin (y = kx). Inverse proportion means the product is constant: multiply one by k and the other is divided by k (xy = c, a decreasing curve). The core learning goals are (1) making the multiplicative structure of direct proportion explicit, distinct from merely additive change, and (2) resisting the 'illusion of proportionality' — the reflex to treat every relationship as directly proportional. Learners should habitually ASK whether doubling one quantity really doubles the other, halves it, or does neither.

activities.title: Proportion lab: drive one quantity, watch the other
feedback: Direct scenario: 'You multiplied pens by 2.5 and the cost multiplied by 2.5 too — the ratio (cost per pen) stayed the same at £1.50, and the line runs straight through (0,0). That is direct proportion.'

Phone-plan scenario: 'You doubled the minutes but the bill did not double — it landed below your guess. The £15 fixed charge is added whatever you do, so at 0 minutes the bill is £15, not £0, and the line misses the origin. This is linear but not proportional.'

Inverse scenario: 'Halving the taps doubled the fill time. Here the bucket's volume is fixed and each tap has the same flow, so the number of taps and the fill time always multiply to the same constant (with one tap taking 60 s, taps × time = 60 s). That constant product, not just one falling as the other rises, is what makes it inverse proportion, and its graph is a curve, not a line.'

If a prediction treats every scenario as doubling: 'Before predicting, ask: if I set this quantity to zero, is the other zero too? That one check separates true proportion from a plan with a fixed charge.'
activities.rationale: Predicting then observing a live recompute makes the multiplicative structure visible and surfaces the illusion of proportionality precisely where it breaks. Contrasting the three scenarios side by side turns the defining property into a checkable question rather than a label. A ratio table shown alongside the graph keeps unit-rate reasoning visible while scaling by multiplication.
sourceClaims: Direct proportion: graph is a straight line through the origin, doubling one quantity doubles the other, and if one quantity is zero the other is zero; children fail to recognise when quantities vary in direct proportion and confuse direct with inverse situations.

A situation such as a phone plan with a fixed monthly charge plus a per-minute rate is linear but NOT proportional (the line does not pass through the origin); students over-apply proportional reasoning ('the numbers dictate the operation').
Distinguishing ratio from proportion and reasoning multiplicatively (unit rate, scaling) rather than additively is the core of proportional reasoning.
learnerActions: Work with three switchable scenarios: pens & cost (4 pens £6 → 10 pens £15, directly proportional); taps filling a bucket or workers digging a hole (inversely proportional); and a phone plan of £15/month + £0.20/min (linear but NOT proportional).
Before changing anything, PREDICT where the next point will land on the graph and what the paired value should be — write or say the prediction and your reason first.
Change quantity A (e.g. with a slider or by choosing a new value) and watch quantity B recompute, with the point plotting live on a graph while a ratio table fills in alongside.

In the phone-plan scenario, double the minutes while predicting the cost will also double; observe that the plotted point lands below your prediction and the traced line clearly does NOT pass through the origin.
In the inverse scenario, halve the number of taps and observe the fill time double, with the curve bending away from the straight line you expected.

Apply two quick tests out loud: 'if one quantity is zero, is the other zero?' (a first check for direct proportion; it is needed but not enough by itself, so also confirm that the ratio stays constant) and 'does doubling one halve the other, keeping the product the same?' (inverse-proportion test).
activities.intendedInsight: Quantity B's response to driving quantity A reveals the structure: in direct proportion the ratio holds (and the line goes through the origin), in inverse proportion the product holds (one goes down as the other goes up), and in linear-but-not-proportional situations a fixed charge means the line misses the origin so doubling fails. Proportionality is a property to test, not a default to assume.

activities.title: Sort situations into direct, inverse, or neither
feedback: If a not-through-origin line is picked as direct proportion: 'Check the start: does this line pass through (0,0)? A line with a fixed starting value is linear but not proportional. Direct proportion must begin at the origin.'

If a ratio table is completed by adding a constant difference: 'From 4 pens to 8 pens you doubled the pens, so double the cost (£6 → £12) rather than adding the same gap. Scale by multiplying — cost per pen stays constant.'

If a 'twice as fast means twice the time' answer appears: 'Picture the taps filling a bucket: more taps means LESS time, not more. One quantity falling as the other rises is not enough on its own, though. It is inverse proportion only if their product stays constant, as taps × time does here.'
activities.rationale: The additive-scaling error and the 'any straight line is proportional' error make sharp, diagnostic distractors, so sorting and selection tasks directly target the known misconceptions. These response formats check discrimination; pair them with the hands-on lab so learners also construct and drive the relationships, not only recognise them.
sourceClaims: Direct proportion: graph is a straight line through the origin, doubling one quantity doubles the other, and if one quantity is zero the other is zero; children fail to recognise when quantities vary in direct proportion and confuse direct with inverse situations.

A situation such as a phone plan with a fixed monthly charge plus a per-minute rate is linear but NOT proportional (the line does not pass through the origin); students over-apply proportional reasoning ('the numbers dictate the operation').
learnerActions: Sort six real-world situations into three bins: directly proportional, inversely proportional, or neither.

For each, justify the placement with a test: for direct proportion, check that the ratio stays constant (so doubling one doubles the other, and zero gives zero); for inverse, check that the product stays constant (so doubling one halves the other). 'Zero gives zero' alone is not enough: a square's side and its area both start at zero, but they are not proportional.
Choose which of several graphs shows direct proportion, deliberately comparing a straight line through the origin against a straight line that misses the origin.
Complete a ratio table for a directly proportional situation by multiplying (scaling columns), and check whether an answer found by adding a fixed difference gives the same result.
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying situations and matching them to graphs forces the discrimination that defines the topic: not every straight line is proportional (it must pass through the origin), and additive scaling is not the same as multiplicative scaling.

activities.title: Reference triptych: three graphs, three tests
feedback: 'The through-origin straight line is the only one of the three showing direct proportion — equal multiplying of both quantities. The offset line is linear but not proportional; the curve shows a constant product (inverse).'
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated reference teaches the recognition cues and supports consolidation. It does not let learners drive a quantity and watch the other respond, so it works best as a reference card after the hands-on lab rather than as the first encounter.
sourceClaims: Direct proportion: graph is a straight line through the origin, doubling one quantity doubles the other, and if one quantity is zero the other is zero; children fail to recognise when quantities vary in direct proportion and confuse direct with inverse situations.
learnerActions: Study a labelled set of three graphs side by side: a straight line through the origin (direct), a smooth decreasing curve (inverse), and a straight line that misses the origin (linear but not proportional).
Reveal, for each graph, its defining property — 'does the line start at (0,0)?' for the lines and 'does the product stay the same?' for the curve.
Use the triptych as a consolidation reference while classifying new situations, checking origin behaviour as a fast first diagnostic.
activities.intendedInsight: For straight-line graphs, origin behaviour is a quick diagnostic: through the origin means direct proportion, and missing the origin means linear but not proportional. A decreasing curve should prompt a check of whether the product stays constant, because not every decreasing curve shows inverse proportion.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain with two taps
feedback: Correct reasoning: 'Sam is wrong. Because of the fixed £15, at 0 minutes the bill is £15, not £0, so the relationship does not pass through the origin. Doubling the minutes only doubles the £0.20-per-minute part: 100 min costs £35, but 200 min costs £55 — less than double £35, which would be £70.'
If 'Sam is right, double is double': 'What does Sam pay if he makes NO calls this month? The £15 at zero minutes shows the line misses the origin, so doubling cannot apply to the whole bill.'

If the bill is said to go DOWN as minutes rise: 'Here more minutes means more cost — both rise together, so it is not inverse. Inverse proportion needs one to fall as the other rises AND their product to stay constant, like taps × fill time.'
If a fixed amount is added again for extra minutes: 'Recompute the variable part: 200 × £0.20 = £40, plus the fixed £15 = £55. The £15 stays put while only the per-minute part scales.'
Counterexample check: 'If there were no £15 charge, just £0.20 per minute, THEN Sam would be right — that version is directly proportional, a line through the origin.'
activities.rationale: Requiring a prediction and a reason before observing makes the diagnostic hinge on reasoning, not just the numerical answer, so the fixed-charge structure is hard to get right for the wrong reason. The taps case and the phone-plan case together separate inverse proportion from linear-but-not-proportional.
sourceClaims: A situation such as a phone plan with a fixed monthly charge plus a per-minute rate is linear but NOT proportional (the line does not pass through the origin); students over-apply proportional reasoning ('the numbers dictate the operation').

Direct proportion: graph is a straight line through the origin, doubling one quantity doubles the other, and if one quantity is zero the other is zero; children fail to recognise when quantities vary in direct proportion and confuse direct with inverse situations.
learnerActions: PREDICT: One tap fills a bucket in 60 seconds. If you open a SECOND tap of the same flow, how long to fill the same bucket? Write your time AND your reason before testing.
OBSERVE: in the idealised model (each tap gives the same constant flow, the bucket volume is fixed, nothing overflows), two taps fill it in 30 seconds.

EXPLAIN: why the naive 'still 60' or '120 seconds' prediction is wrong — twice the taps gives HALF the time because taps and time are inversely proportional: the bucket's volume (total water) is fixed and each tap has equal flow, so the number of taps × the fill time stays constant, meaning doubling the taps halves the time.

Then tackle the phone-plan question: a plan costs £15/month plus £0.20 per minute. Sam says 'if I talk for twice as many minutes, my bill will be twice as big.' Decide whether Sam is right and explain how you know.

Probe deeper: What would Sam pay for 0 minutes, and what does that say about proportionality? Work out the bill for 100 minutes and for 200 minutes — is the second exactly double the first? What if the plan had no £15 charge — would Sam be right then? And is 'twice as many taps' the same kind of relationship as the phone bill?
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a reason before observing exposes the illusion of proportionality: a learner who truly grasps direct proportion tests the origin ('what happens at zero?') and sees that the fixed charge breaks the doubling rule, while a learner running the reflex answers 'twice the bill' automatically.

constraints: Delay the formulae y = kx and xy = c until ratio-table and product-constancy reasoning is secure, so learners reason about structure rather than substituting into a memorised triangle.
Scale direct-proportion tables by multiplying, never by adding a constant difference.
Build direct proportion from ratio tables and double number lines so the unit rate (e.g. cost per pen) stays visible.

Selection and sorting tasks check whether a learner can discriminate the three families, but recognition-only responses do not require the learner to construct or drive a relationship; pair them with the hands-on predict-and-drive work.
The fixed reference triptych shows cues and supports consolidation but cannot let a learner vary one quantity and watch the other respond; treat it as a reference, not the first encounter.

When using the taps/inverse example, state the idealisation (equal constant flow per tap, fixed bucket volume, no overflow) and be precise that the constant product is taps × time (equal to the one-tap fill time, 60 s), not the volume itself.

Optional interaction examples (a slider driving a value, a live-plotting point, a ratio table filling alongside, tap-to-reveal properties) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory; the essential requirements are prediction-before-observation and side-by-side contrast of the three families.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-audit of arithmetic: phone plan £15 + £0.20/min gives 100 min → £15 + £20 = £35 and 200 min → £15 + £40 = £55; £55 is less than double £35 (which would be £70), confirming non-proportionality. Pens: 4 → 10 is ×2.5 with cost £6 → £15 (ratio £1.50/pen held). These figures are consistent across the activities and the source's assessment.

Independent re-audit of the taps/inverse claim: the original source phrasing 'their product, the total water, is fixed' is imprecise. What is fixed is the bucket's volume; given equal flow per tap, t = 60/n so the number of taps × the fill time is the constant 60 s (equal to the one-tap fill time), not the volume. The learner-facing text avoids equating the product with the volume.
The idealisation behind the taps example (equal constant flow, fixed volume, no overflow) is stated in the activity and constraint.

The source's artefact-fit entries asserted that in-role dialogue 'adds no persona-grounded value' and that 3D 'adds a dimension the concept does not have.' These are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws; they have been dropped rather than propagated as universal claims. The planar, tabular/graphical nature of the relationship is retained as a design rationale without claiming other media cannot teach it.

assess.poeTask: PREDICT: One tap fills a bucket in 60 seconds. If you open a SECOND tap of the same flow, how long to fill the same bucket? Write your time and WHY before testing. OBSERVE: two taps fill it in 30 seconds. EXPLAIN: the naive 'still 60' or '120' prediction is violated — twice the taps gives HALF the time because the taps and time are INVERSELY proportional (their product, total water, is fixed), not directly proportional. The stated reason before observing is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: What would Sam pay for 0 minutes? What does that tell you about whether the bill is proportional to the minutes?
Work out the bill for 100 minutes and for 200 minutes — is the second exactly double the first? Why not?
What if the plan had NO £15 monthly charge, just £0.20 a minute — would Sam be right THEN? (counterexample: this version IS directly proportional, line through origin.)
Now think about filling a bucket: if you use twice as many taps, does it take twice as long, or half as long? Is that the same kind of relationship as the phone bill?
assess.correctAnswer: Sam is wrong. The bill is NOT directly proportional to the minutes because of the fixed £15 charge: at 0 minutes the bill is £15, not £0, so the relationship does not pass through the origin. Doubling the minutes doubles only the £0.20-per-minute part, not the whole bill — e.g. 100 min costs £35, but 200 min costs £55, which is less than double.

errorPatterns.pattern: Illusion of proportionality — 'twice the minutes, twice the bill', treating every relationship as directly proportional and ignoring the fixed £15 charge
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what does Sam pay if he makes NO calls this month?' — the £15 at zero minutes exposes that the line misses the origin, so doubling can't apply to the whole bill. Sort more situations by the zero test.
errorPatterns.distractor: Sam is right — if the minutes double then the bill doubles too
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'Sam is right' and, when asked, says 'because double is double' without ever considering the cost at zero minutes

errorPatterns.pattern: Confusing inverse with direct — thinking 'twice as many minutes' might HALVE something, misreading which quantity grows
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two families explicitly: here more minutes means MORE cost (both rise), so it is not inverse; inverse is when one rises as the other falls. Contrast with a taps-filling-a-bucket case.
errorPatterns.distractor: Sam is wrong — doubling the minutes actually halves part of the bill
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about the bill going down or getting smaller when minutes increase, conflating this with a 'twice as fast, half the time' situation

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive scaling — adds a fixed amount to the bill for the extra minutes rather than reasoning multiplicatively about the per-minute rate
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to a ratio table for the per-minute part only; show the variable part scales multiplicatively while the £15 stays put. Reteach unit-rate scaling on the pens&cost case.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to find the bill for 200 minutes having been told 100 minutes, adds the same £20 gap again instead of recomputing 200×£0.20+£15

responseLevels.gap: Says Sam is right ('double is double') or reasons only additively; does not consider the cost at zero minutes and cannot distinguish proportional from non-proportional situations.
responseLevels.full: States Sam is wrong BECAUSE the £15 fixed charge means the relationship does not pass through the origin, so doubling the minutes does not double the whole bill; confirms with 100→£35, 200→£55, and correctly identifies that removing the fixed charge would make it directly proportional while a bucket-and-taps case is inverse.
responseLevels.partial: Recognises something is off or can compute 100 vs 200 minutes, but explains it as arithmetic ('I just worked it out') without articulating the origin/fixed-charge structure, and cannot reliably sort a new situation into direct / inverse / neither.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A phone plan costs £15 each month plus £0.20 for every minute you call. Sam says: 'If I talk for twice as many minutes, my bill will be twice as big.' Is Sam right? Explain how you know.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who truly grasps direct proportion tests the origin ('what happens at zero minutes?') and sees the fixed charge breaks the doubling rule — they cannot be talked out of it. A child running the illusion of proportionality hears 'twice the minutes' and answers 'twice the bill' automatically; the fixed charge is invisible to them. The two children give different answers AND different reasons, and the fixed-charge structure makes it hard to be right for the wrong reason.
